newsitem.title: CHINA: China premier sees 8 pct growth, state firm reform.
newsitem.headline: China premier sees 8 pct growth, state firm reform.

text.p: Demonstrating business as usual in China after the death of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, Premier Li Peng will issue an annual report setting 8.0 percent growth and tackling reform of lumbering state firms.

In his report at the opening of the National People's Congress, or parliament, on Saturday, Li will vow to pursue Deng's sweeping market reforms, hailing a booming economy while warning that losses by state firms threaten China's future.
"The national economy has continued to show faster growth, inflation has effectively been controlled," Li will tell more than 2,900 parliamentary deputies.
"This is one of the outstanding features of the economy of last year," Li says in the speech, his annual government work report, parts of which were seen by Reuters on Friday.
Li will set the target for economic growth at 8.0 percent, which for China is cautious.
He set a similar target last year but China's sizzling economy, spurred by Deng's market reforms launched 18 years ago, defied Li's bid for caution and grew by 9.7 percent in 1996.

Li has been one of China's strongest proponents of slowing economic growth, albeit with limited success, following three years of double-digit increases in the early 1990s when the economy showed signs of overheating. The State Statistical Bureau has forecast 10.5 percent growth for this year.

For the first time in years, Li no longer ranks inflation as China's biggest problem and focuses much of his report on how to force loss-making state firms to adapt to the market place -- to show a profit or go under.
Li warned that without reform of state enterprises, two-thirds of which are in the red, China's socialist system could crumble.

"The development and reform of state enterprises is a major economic problem that relates to the nation's economic development and is also a major political problem that relates to the fate of the socialist system," Li says.

China's estimated 100,000 state firms reported the first ever net loss in the first quarter of last year, and while they have since recovered slightly, officials warn that they remain a major burden on the economy.

To nurture state firms that do make a profit, Li pledged to expand to 511 from 300 the number of big firms that receive priority for loans, and to increase the cities chosen as pilots for implementing bankruptcies and mergers to 110 from 58.

China has been loath to force state firms to sink or swim in the marketplace, unwilling to confront a shift away from the socialist tenet of public ownership while raising the spectre of bankruptcy, unemployment and possible social unrest.
Growth in investment in fixed assets should not exceed 32 percent, Li said.
He would persist with an "appropriately" tight monetary policy -- easing slightly from a squeeze imposed more than three years ago -- and would have to be alert to inflation, Li said.
China's benchmark retail inflation fell to 6.1 percent last year, compared with 14.8 percent in 1995 and a communist-era high of 21.7 percent the year before.
Li's stand on the fledgling securities and futures markets offered little shift from a three-year crackdown.
"We must regulate the securities and futures market and increase our sense of risk," Li said.
